Text: Vowel quality is {{c1::which particular sound a vowel has}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: "The pronunciation of alif has a similar range; we refer to these differences in pronunciation as vowel quality."

Distinguish: vowel quality is which sound the vowel is — the e of bet, the a of bat, the u of but; vowel length is how long the vowel is held.

Why: two things shift the quality of alif — the speaker's regional dialect (deeper, like father, in the Arabian Peninsula and Iraq; more frontal, toward the e of bet, in North Africa) and the surrounding consonants.

Text: Besides vowel quality, Arabic also distinguishes vowel {{c1::length}}, and this too can change a word's meaning.
Back Extra:
Ex: DHaalim — a long alif in the first syllable, a short i in the second.

Distinguish: quality is which vowel sound you make (a frontal or a deep alif); length is how long you hold it — Arabic keeps track of both.

Cue: alif itself is a long vowel — the one you hear held in DHaalim.

Text: In Arabic, word stress is attracted to the syllable with a {{c1::long::long or short}} vowel.
Back Extra:
Ex: DHaalim — the accent falls on the first syllable, the one with the long alif, not on the short i of the second.

Distinguish: vowel length is a property of one vowel (long or short); word stress is a property of the whole word (which syllable carries the accent).
